messages.body_plain:
It looks like you are trying to fit a bifactor model, which usually requires specifying the factors to be uncorrelated in order to achieve identification. You can do this by fixing the F1 F2 F3 intercorrelations to 0.

Hope that helps!
Elliot

messages.subject: Re: Issues of "usermodel"
messages.body_plain:
Hi Shaokang,

It doesn't look like there is anything inherently problematic with that model, but the bifactor model is one of the more finicky ones that may have convergence problems when the pattern of variances and covariances is highly divergent from what is expected under the bifactor.

I suggest that you ensure that the SNP heritabiliteis are nontrivial (check diag of S matrix), that the pattern of genetic correlations includes sizable associations among the variables (check the off diag of the standardized S matrix, after standardizing using cov2cor). For instance, if one of the phenotypes is not genetically correlated with any of the other phenotypes, then a bifactor model may be problematic.

You might also start by fitting some simpler models to see if they converge. For instance a 1 factor model would be worth testing. You could then go on to specify two correlated factors, for the A and B phenotypes. If that converges but the correlation bewteen the two factors is very close to 0, that would suggest that adding in the general factor may not be warranted.

Cheers,

Elliot

messages.body_plain:
Dear Shaokang,
It looks like the correlation between the two factors in your model is estimated at just above 1.0, which suggests that the factors can be combined into a single factor. The bifactor model may be failing because you are attempting  two fit those two domain-specific factors in addition to the single general factor. In otherwords, your prespecified confirmatory model may not be appropriate for the data. You can consider other theoretially-driven models or you might move on to running models that are informed by exploratory methods, such as PCA or EFA. For instance, you can obtain the eigen vectors from the eigen decomposition that you've performed and use them to guide model specification within the Genomic SEM framework. There of course is the potential for overfitting if you take such an exploratory approach.
Cheers,
Elliot

The bifactor model may be failing because you are attempting  two fit those two domain-specific factors in addition to the single general factor. In otherwords, your prespecified confirmatory model may not be appropriate for the data. You can consider other theoretially-driven models or you might move on to running models that are informed by exploratory methods, such as PCA or EFA. For instance, you can obtain the eigen vectors from the eigen decomposition that you've performed and use them to guide model specification within the Genomic SEM framework. There of course is the potential for overfitting if you take such an exploratory approach.
> Cheers,

messages.subject: Re: non-human species
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tianhua,

The ldsc function is currently set-up to work for human populations with respect to assumptions about LD structure and overall selection. In general, you would not be able to do cross-species models (e.g., different types of plant barley) because the LD structures would presumably change across the different types of plants. If you are working within a single species and have LD-scores for that population than the program can be used with non-human populations. With that said you would want to put some careful thought into some of the assumptions of the model and ideally run some simulations or use a trait for which you know what the SNP heritability (h2) should be to see that you are getting numbers close the expected value. The original developers of ld-score regression have also responded to similar questions on their google group (links to those responses below).

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/ldsc_users/cUVUcJifhSU/0EhqROm7gJgJ;context-place=msg/ldsc_users/Nag-yNFm1Mo/NWVgM6JSBQAJ

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/ldsc_users/Nag-yNFm1Mo/NWVgM6JSBQAJ

-Andrew

messages.subject: Re: Error in sumstats()
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nora,

sumsats, depending on your input, may actually be plowing trough 9 million+ lines of summary statistics, this can be fairly slow depending on your machine. The usual solution is to split the files into pieces (per chromosome for example) and to run the chromosomes in parallel on a cluster.

To make sure there is no other issue here, you could make files that contain like 10 SNPs (or even just 2) and see if those run. If they do run you need to either wait longer or run per chromosome, if they don't come back here and we'll figure out whats wrong.

Best,
Michel
